rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two sons of Adam in the story are Cain and Abel, also known from Genesis 4:1–16.
rows.anchor: the story of Cain and Abel, mentioned in Genesis iv, 1-16

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “tell them” refers to the followers of the Bible and connects the passage with 5:15.
rows.anchor: The pronoun in "tell them" refers to the followers of the Bible, and obviously connects with verse 15 of this surah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the Bible followers’ concealed moral in the story is summarized in 5:32.
rows.anchor: The moral of this particular Biblical story - a moral which the followers of the Bible have been "concealing from themselves" - is summarized in verse 32.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although nafs can mean soul, mind, or self, Asad reads it here as desire or passionate determination and prefers “passion,” citing Qamus and Zamakhshari’s Asas.
rows.anchor: Among the many meanings attributable to the noun nafs (primarily, "soul", or "mind", or "self"), there is also that of "desire" or "passionate determination"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged partners are supposed to share in God's divinity by protecting or helping those who invoke them; Asad refers to 6:22, note 15.
rows.anchor: whom you supposed to be [God's] partners with regard to you - i.e., being able, in result of their alleged "share in God's divinity", to protect or help you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The things that have vanished are the imagined intercessors or mediators between humanity and God.
rows.anchor: all that you were wont to assert [or "to suppose"] has gone away from you" - i.e., all the imaginary intercessors or mediators between man and God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence describes gradual human development, both from embryo to full individual existence and across the evolution of the human race.
rows.anchor: is meant to bring out the fact of man's gradual development, in the individual sense, from the embryonic stage to full-fledged existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad treats God's command that the angels prostrate before Adam as allegorical and points to 2:30–34 and its notes.
rows.anchor: As regards God's allegorical command to the angels to "prostrate themselves" before Adam, see 2:30-34

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the passage first addresses all mankind, Adam's name here symbolizes the whole human race.
rows.anchor: his name symbolizes, in this context, the whole human race

rows.speaker: Western scholars
rows.claim: Western scholars commonly regard Iblis as a corruption of the Greek diabolos, from which English “devil” derives.
rows.anchor: Western scholars usually take it for granted that the name "Iblis" is a corruption of the Greek word diabolos

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad rejects the Greek-borrowing claim: there is no evidence that pre-Islamic Arabs borrowed such terms from Greeks, while Greek mythology drew substantially on earlier South Arabian civilization.
rows.anchor: There is, however, not the slightest evidence that the pre-Islamic Arabs borrowed this or any other mythological term from the Greeks

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad proposes that Greek diabolos Hellenized Arabic Iblis, derived from ablasa (“despaired,” “gave up hope,” or “became broken in spirit”); Greek familiarity could explain the association despite the word’s Greek origin.
rows.anchor: One may, therefore, assume with something approaching certainty that the Greek diabolos is a Hellenized form of the Arabic name for the Fallen Angel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to his note on 38:76 for Iblis's claim in the next verse that he was created from fire.
rows.anchor: As regards Iblis' statement, in the next verse, that he had been created "out of fire", see surah 38. note 60.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to the parallel accounts and notes at 2:35 and 20:120.
rows.anchor: See 2:35 and 20:120, as well as the corresponding notes.

words: لِيُبْدِىَ لَهُمَا مَا وُۥرِىَ عَنْهُمَا مِن سَوْءَٰتِهِمَا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unveiling of their nakedness allegorizes pre-fall innocence; consciousness then brings self-awareness and choice between actions, with temptations to evil and misery following a wrong choice.
rows.anchor: an allegory of the state of innocence in which man lived before his fall from grace

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase literally as becoming among those who endure.
rows.anchor: or [lest] you become of those who are enduring

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan tempts them with the desire to live forever and thereby become like God; Asad links this to 20:120, note 106.
rows.anchor: thus instilling in them the desire to live forever and to become in this respect, like God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wajh, literally “face,” can figuratively mean a person's entire being or attention; Asad cites the phrase in 3:20 as an example.
rows.anchor: The term wajh (lit., "face") occurring here is often used, in the abstract sense, to denote a person's entire being or entire attention

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although masjid usually means the time or place of prostration, here and in 7:31 it signifies any act of worship.
rows.anchor: evidently stands in this context - as well as in verse 31 below - for any act of worship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like the Thamud-inhabited harrah, the adjoining region of Madyan (Biblical Midian) shows abundant evidence of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.
rows.anchor: Like the harrah once inhabited by the Thamud tribe, the adjoining region of Madyan (the Biblical Midian) shows ample evidence of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that they might return to righteousness.
rows.anchor: Lit., "so that they might return [to righteousness]".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads “servants” as created beings subject to God's will, including living or dead saints and inanimate objects such as idols, fetishes, and physical or mental images of saints or deified persons.
rows.anchor: This refers to saints living or dead, as well as to inanimate objects of every description

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the summons as calling upon the supposed divine partners and refers to 6:22, note 15.
rows.anchor: Lit., "summon your [God-]partners" (see surah 6, note 15).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those with your Sustainer” metaphorically describes utter God-consciousness.
rows.anchor: a metaphorical description of utter God-consciousness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Desisting means abandoning efforts to turn others from God's path and stopping the war against believers.
rows.anchor: from their endeavour to turn others away from the path of God and from waging war against the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means the example of earlier peoples; it alludes to disasters that have overtaken and will overtake those who persistently deny moral truths.
rows.anchor: the example (sunnah) of the people of old times has already come to pass

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites' behavior is effectively the reverse of what is expected of believers; Asad cites 3:104, 3:110, 3:114, 9:71, 9:112, and 22:41.
rows.anchor: their behaviour is - in its effect, at least - the exact opposite of that expected of the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses concern deliberate hypocrites identified in 9:66, not wavering people whose hypocrisy arises from inner fears and uncertainty.
rows.anchor: this and the following verses refer to the conscious hypocrites spoken of in the last sentence of the preceding verse, and not to the waverers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes an alternative rendering of the believers' awliya' as “protectors” or “friends and protectors” of one another.
rows.anchor: Or: "are the protectors [or "friends and protectors"] of one another".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad prefers the primary sense “near” or “close” to one another because believers are contrasted with hypocrites described as all alike in 9:67.
rows.anchor: preferable to render the term wali (of which awliya' is the plural) in its primary meaning of being "near" or "close" to one another
